fatal_errors: The proposed dominant mechanism is thermally activated overcoming of Peierls barriers, whereas the target attributes yielding to stress-drop-associated nucleation of Shockley partial dislocations at vacancy clusters or locally disordered atoms.

The intervention uses conventional experimental strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1 rather than the molecular-dynamics range of 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1, so its strain-rate-insensitivity claim is not bounded to the regime actually studied.
The structural-mediator description incorrectly includes Co even though the specified alloy is FeNiCrMn.
The orientation design does not reconstruct the tested <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> directions or the finding that <-111> has the maximum yield stress.
explanation: The hypothesis captures several broad outcomes: FCC single-crystal behavior, temperature-dependent yield softening, weak yield-rate sensitivity, dislocation-mediated plasticity, and absence of an FCC-to-BCC transformation. However, it misses the central defect-specific mechanism and instead assigns rate insensitivity to a generic Peierls-barrier thermal-activation model. It also substitutes an incompatible experimental strain-rate regime and omits the target orientation set and anisotropic ranking. The proposed in-situ XRD/TEM test is reasonably discriminating for a BCC transformation and could be strengthened by explicitly resolving Shockley partials and stacking-fault-induced HCP-like regions. The cited evidence is weak because it mainly concerns Co-containing nanowires, unrelated BCC alloys, or broader HEA systems rather than bulk single-crystal FeNiCrMn under the target MD conditions.
